Re-checked all of it against the current tree. Score: **two findings stand, one I raised is now properly fixed, one I was too harsh on, and the new code holds up better than I expected.**

## Still wrong — both unchanged, both uncited

**1. The 28–37% working-length figure survived the merge.** `DOMAIN_KNOWLEDGE.md:257–258` still reads *"Changing working length alone shifts axial stiffness by 28–37%"* with no source. Contradicted by **Hoffmeier 2011 ([PMID 21185629](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21185629/))**: stiffness unchanged between short and medium working length, **reduced 10%** at long. **Chen 2026 ([PMID 41688946](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41688946/))** confirms the direction on a femoral shaft under single-leg stance but quotes no such percentage. Still a locked file shipped to Devin as authoritative.

**2. The dog-radius study is still uncited** at line 241–242. It's real and described accurately — **Mie et al. 2020, *PLoS One*, [PMID 32877422](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32877422/)**. Adding the PMID costs one line and converts an assertion into evidence.

## I was right to flag it — and they fixed it properly

My critique said: *"if you recalibrate the stress model, re-verify that uniform thickening still fails."* The retune (`b16314b`) did exactly that, and better than I asked. `design_space_note` now reports a **measured sweep** over the full legal space instead of arithmetic:

| | |
|---|---|
| Baseline 180×16×3.0 | **914 MPa** |
| Best constant-thickness design *anywhere* legal | **396 MPa** — 13% over |
| Variable-thickness, same 55 g | **316 MPa** — passes |

It even names the window's edges: at 50 g nothing passes, at 60 g a plain constant plate passes and the argument collapses. And it carries a `HISTORY` line admitting the old 412 MPa figure came from `stub.py` while the real validator returned SKIP.

That's the honest version. The scalar escape is closed, and now demonstrably rather than rhetorically.

## Where I was too harsh

I said your femur was "more curved than average" and implied overclaiming. `make_bone.py:36–37` actually states 0.91 m is *"inside the published femoral range (~0.8–1.5 m)"* — which is a fair framing, and my PubMed hits bracket it sensibly (452 mm distal femur, Liaw 2019; 772 mm severely bowed, Park 2016). It sits at the curved end of normal, which the file doesn't hide. Withdraw the criticism.

## New code, checked against literature — holds up

**`hole_kt()` is correctly sourced.** Heywood's net-section correlation `Kt = 2 + (1 − d/W)³`, named in the docstring rather than buried as a magic 2.4. At d/W→0 it gives **Kt = 3**, matching the textbook value for a hole in a wide plate. It also deliberately uses the *tension* factor where out-of-plane bending would give ~1.8–2.0 — conservative on purpose, and it says so.

**The load retune is better supported than I assumed.** I went in suspicious that 15 → 7 N·m was difficulty-tuning dressed as physiology. Then **Lu et al. 1997 ([PMID 9456377](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9456377/))** — instrumented femoral prostheses, telemetered in vivo — concludes that bending is carried largely by muscle tension plus bone compression, so *"moments transmitted by the bones are smaller than the limb moments."* A low plate bending moment is physiologically defensible, not a fudge. The same paper's force magnification ratios (1.3–29.8) also support 3×BW axial as reasonable.

## One new problem the code admits to itself

`case.json`'s `axis_note` says it outright: **"+X is both lateral (case, generator) and anterior (make_bone bow), and those cannot both be true."**

I confirmed it — `make_bone.py` returns `bow(s) + radius(s)` along **+X**, so the *anterior* bow is modelled on the *lateral* face the plate mounts to. Anatomically the femoral bow is sagittal (anterior), while plates go lateral, and every paper I found (Liaw, Park) treats bowing as sagittal. So the conformance failure driving your whole demo is currently geometrically real but anatomically mislabelled.

The validator hedges by computing both bending planes and reporting the worse — sound engineering. But the frame contradiction is the one thing here a clinician in the audience would catch, and it's stated in your own locked input file rather than resolved.

## Also still true

`_OK_STATUSES = (PASS, SKIP)` is unchanged. Far less dangerous now that stress is real — only `screw_pullout_min` returns SKIP, and for a genuinely good reason (pull-out depends on locked bone and screw inputs; no plate change can move it, so reporting a number "would be theatre"). That reasoning is correct. But the mechanism still means any future unimplemented check silently passes.

content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in. Format is part of this read — decided, not defaulted: a Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title and takes almost none of the craft below, so it fits only when the user asked for Markdown or the content is bound for a Markdown-native destination; never pick it to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the one font host the Artifact CSP admits — link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=…&display=swap">`); a face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI or it falls back silently. Either way, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* — most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token — a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Before publishing, scan the stylesheet for any color declared only inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — that is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject — or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name — a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word — a greeting, a category, a page-type label — the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

Design plan before I build:

**Palette** — warm bone-white ground `#F7F6F3`, cool near-black ink `#16181A`, one accent of deep **surgical teal** `#0F5C57` (teal is the colour of surgical drapes for a real reason — it's the complement of blood red), and amber `#A8641E` reserved *semantically* for unproven claims, never decoration.

**Type** — Newsreader for display (a journal serif, not the safe grotesque), Source Sans 3 for body, IBM Plex Mono for figures and PMIDs.

**Layout** — the opinionated call: a persistent **evidence rail**. Every claim sits beside either its citation or an explicit "not measured" marker. The page's structure enacts the project's own thesis — a claim without verification is visibly incomplete.

Impact assessment · Munich Agentic Hackathon · TUM.ai

The bottleneck was never the printer. It was the engineer.

Patient-specific bone plates have been technically possible for a decade. They stay rare because every one costs an engineer days of CAD work and an analyst's simulation time. Printing is cheap, titanium is a commodity, and the physics runs in milliseconds. What does not scale is a human authoring geometry, one patient at a time. That is the cost this project attacks, and it is the only claim on this page that the literature already supports.

A

Where the cost actually sits today

Four findings from the published record, and none of them is about machines being slow.

Off-the-shelf plates are bent by hand, in theatre

A surgeon contours a straight plate to the patient's bone during the operation. It consumes operating time under anaesthesia, the result varies with who is holding the benders, and repeated cold bending of titanium is not free — it work-hardens the material and can notch it at exactly the point where the plate later has to survive millions of cycles.

Jo et al. 2023, Sci RepCustomised 3D-printed pelvic plate compared against the conventional bending process · PMID 37386116

"Pre-contoured" does not mean it fits

Manufacturers ship anatomically pre-shaped plates, and researchers keep publishing studies measuring how badly they still fit real people. Anatomical variation is the whole problem: a shape averaged over a population is, by construction, wrong for nearly every individual in it.

Lorsuwannarat & Jirangkul 2026Anatomical compatibility of pre-contoured clavicular locking plates, patient-specific 3D modelling · PMID 41718820 Gryska et al. 2024Standard volar plates do not fit malunited distal radii — a shim instrument built to work around it · PMID 38747532

Custom implants are rationed to extreme cases

Where the anatomy leaves no alternative — tumour resection, craniofacial reconstruction, spinal replacement — patient-specific implants are already routine and clearly work. They are not used for a common shaft fracture because the design labour per case cannot be justified, not because the engineering is unsolved.

Choy et al. 2017Personalised 3D-printed vertebral body after tumour resection · PMID 28578109 Spetzger et al. 2016Individualised cervical fusion cage, planning to implantation · PMID 26931333

Optimisation already solves the numbers — a human still decides the shape

Topology optimisation for fracture plates is a mature field with a decade of results. Every one of those studies is a research project: a human frames the problem, defines the design space, runs the solver, interprets the output. The solver sizes what it is given. It does not decide that this plate needs a rib at mid-span and that one needs its head split.

Moosabeiki et al. 20233D-printed patient-specific plates: topology optimisation vs conventional design · PMID 37866280 Al-Tamimi 2021Topology-optimised locking compression plates to reduce stress shielding · PMID 34286146
B

What an autonomous loop changes

Three separate economies, and they are worth keeping apart because they scale differently. None of the figures below are measured on this system yet — section D says exactly which numbers are still missing.

Time

Calendar → clock

A human design review loop is bounded by working hours: propose, simulate, wait, meet, revise. An agent loop is bounded by compute. It runs overnight, unattended, and the iteration budget is a number in a config file rather than a scheduling problem.

The reduction is not "faster CAD". It is removing the human from the critical path between iterations, so elapsed time stops being dominated by when people are awake.

Money

~200:1SWEEP : AGENT TURN

The design work splits in two. Shape decisions — rib or no rib, split the head, route further around the bone — need judgement, and cost one agent turn each. Dimension decisions — exact thickness, exact fillet radius — are arithmetic, and a numeric optimiser answers a few hundred of them for the price of one turn.

Getting that split right is what makes the loop affordable: roughly five expensive decisions instead of forty.

Logistics

Inventory → file

A hospital currently stocks many plate lengths and shapes per anatomy, plus the bending instruments, and still sometimes lacks the right one. Patient-specific manufacture replaces a physical catalogue with a design file and a printer.

The second logistical gain is documentary: the commit history is the design history file — which check failed, what changed, what was rejected, what the numbers did after. That artefact is mandatory for a real device and normally costs dedicated effort.

C

What it changes for the operation itself

A plate that already fits

The geometry is contoured to this patient's bone before it is manufactured, so the contouring step leaves the operating room entirely. Fit stops depending on how much time is available and who is doing the bending.

Zeng et al. 2016, InjuryPre-bent plates shaped to the individual pelvis via 3D printing and virtual planning · PMID 27372187

Fit that is deliberately imperfect

A plate pressed flat against bone crushes the periosteum and interrupts the blood supply the fracture heals through — which is why limited-contact plates exist at all. The verifier bounds the bone gap from both sides: at most 1.5 mm, and at least 0.1 mm. Zero clearance is recorded as a failure, not an optimum.

Kregor et al. 1995, J Orthop ResLC-DCP designed to reduce cortical contact, ischaemia and porosis · PMID 7472750

Strength is a window, not a maximum

The intuitive fix for a failing stress check — make it thicker — produces a clinically worse device. An over-stiff plate carries load the bone should carry, the bone underneath resorbs, and the construct fails later by a different route. That failure mode is documented in a 3D-printed titanium plate specifically, so the constraint set treats stiffness as a band with both bounds binding.

  • No cost or wall-clock figure per validated design. We have not yet measured compute cost per iteration, so the 200:1 ratio above is the designed intent of the two-tier split, not an observed result.
  • No operating-room time saved. The mechanism is sound and the fit literature supports it, but we have measured nothing in a theatre and will not claim minutes.
  • Synthetic anatomy. One procedurally generated femur. No patient data, no clinical validation, no FDA / ISO / ASTM claim of any kind.
  • Analytical stress model, not FEA. Beam theory over cross-sections measured off the exported solid, with Heywood's net-section factor at the holes. Fast and honest about being a surrogate — but a confirming finite-element solve has not been run.
  • No fatigue analysis. Bone plates fail by fatigue, not single overload. The safety factor of 2.5 exists to cover that, and a cyclic analysis is not a substitute for it — neither has been performed.
  • A claim in our own domain document is unsourced. It states that working length shifts axial stiffness by 28–37%. We could not find that figure, and the closest controlled study reports 10%. The direction is right; the magnitude is currently unsupported and flagged for correction.
E

Taking it further

Ordered by what unblocks what. The first phase turns claims above into measurements; the later ones widen the domain.

Phase 1
Immediate

Close the evidence gaps

  • One confirming FEA solve on the final design — tetrahedral mesh, mesh-convergence table. The surrogate steers, the solver confirms.
  • A simulated standard bench test. Four-point bending per the established metallic bone-plate method, reported as an engineer would receive it.
  • Instrument the loop. Cost and elapsed time per validated design, so section B stops being an argument and becomes a number.
Phase 2
Near term

From one case to a population

  • Real CT ingestion end to end — segmentation, anatomical frame, quality gate — so the input is a scan rather than a generated mesh.
  • Batch across many patients unattended, which is the only way to show generality rather than a single lucky convergence.
  • Fatigue as a first-class check, since it is the real failure mode.
  • The verifier as a network service the agent holds no credentials to, making the trust boundary physical rather than procedural.
Phase 3
Beyond

Other anatomies, other species, other domains

  • More anatomy — the pipeline takes a mesh and a plan, so a different bone is a different input rather than a different program.
  • Vision in the loop. Render the stress field onto the part and let the agent look at it. A coordinate is not actionable; a picture of where the plate narrows is.
  • Parallel design strategies. When one approach stalls, try three structurally different ones at once and keep the best — recording the losers, which is itself evidence.
F

Where else this goes

Veterinary orthopaedics

The strongest near-term application, and not as a consolation prize. Anatomical variation across breeds and species destroys the economics of standard inventory — a plate range that covers a dachshund and a great dane does not exist. Proven domain

Adjacent

Any design problem with a frozen scorer

That pattern applies wherever correctness is measurable and gaming the metric is the easy path — brackets, housings, heat sinks, fixtures.

## The argument I built it around

The strongest honest claim isn't "we save X%". It's **the bottleneck was never the printer — it was the engineer.** Titanium is a commodity, printing is cheap, your physics runs in milliseconds. - Plates get **bent by hand in theatre** (Jo 2023 explicitly benchmarks against "the conventional bending process")

That last one is the thesis: the gap in the literature is exactly the gap your project fills.

## The design decision worth knowing about

Every claim sits beside an **evidence rail** — either its PubMed citation, or an amber marker saying no evidence exists yet. The layout enacts your own thesis: a claim without verification is visibly incomplete. Same reason your UI can't render a SKIP as a pass.

Which leads to **section D, "What we have not measured"** — I'd argue it's the most persuasive thing on the page. It lists, in amber, that you have no cost-per-design figure, no OR-time measurement, synthetic anatomy only, no FEA, no fatigue analysis — **and that a claim in your own domain doc is unsourced and contradicted by a 10% finding.** Volunteering that before a judge finds it converts a weakness into evidence of rigour. It also inoculates you: nobody can catch you out on something you listed yourself.

**No invented ROI.** Not one fabricated euro or minute. The only ratio on the page is 200:1 optimiser-evals-per-agent-turn, and it's labelled as designed intent rather than an observed result, because you haven't measured ACUs yet.

# Autonomous Fixation — impact and roadmap

Impact assessment for the Munich Agentic Hackathon (TUM.ai), Cognition / Devin track.
Source material for the presentation and the website copy.

> **The bottleneck was never the printer. It was the engineer.**
>
> Patient-specific bone plates have been technically possible for a decade. They stay rare
> because every one costs an engineer days of CAD work and an analyst's simulation time.
> Printing is cheap, titanium is a commodity, and the physics runs in milliseconds. What does
> not scale is a human authoring geometry, one patient at a time. That is the cost this
> project attacks, and it is the only claim here that the literature already supports.

Every claim below is either **cited** to a PubMed record, marked **architectural** (a property
of the system, not a measured result), or listed in [section D](#d--what-we-have-not-measured)
as unproven. Nothing is estimated silently.

---

## A · Where the cost actually sits today

Four findings from the published record, and none of them is about machines being slow.

### Off-the-shelf plates are bent by hand, in theatre

A surgeon contours a straight plate to the patient's bone during the operation. It consumes
operating time under anaesthesia, the result varies with who is holding the benders, and
repeated cold bending of titanium is not free — it work-hardens the material and can notch it
at exactly the point where the plate later has to survive millions of cycles.

> **Jo et al. 2023, *Sci Rep*** — customised 3D-printed pelvic plate compared against the
> conventional bending process. [PMID 37386116](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37386116/)

### "Pre-contoured" does not mean it fits

Manufacturers ship anatomically pre-shaped plates, and researchers keep publishing studies
measuring how badly they still fit real people. Anatomical variation is the whole problem: a
shape averaged over a population is, by construction, wrong for nearly every individual in it.

> **Lorsuwannarat & Jirangkul 2026** — anatomical compatibility of pre-contoured clavicular
> locking plates, patient-specific 3D modelling. [PMID 41718820](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41718820/)
>
> **Gryska et al. 2024** — standard volar plates do not fit malunited distal radii; a shim
> instrument was built to work around it. [PMID 38747532](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38747532/)

### Custom implants are rationed to extreme cases

Where the anatomy leaves no alternative — tumour resection, craniofacial reconstruction,
spinal replacement — patient-specific implants are already routine and clearly work. They are
not used for a common shaft fracture because the design labour per case cannot be justified,
not because the engineering is unsolved.

> **Choy et al. 2017** — personalised 3D-printed vertebral body after tumour resection.
> [PMID 28578109](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28578109/)
>
> **Spetzger et al. 2016** — individualised cervical fusion cage, planning to implantation.
> [PMID 26931333](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26931333/)

### Optimisation already solves the numbers — a human still decides the shape

Topology optimisation for fracture plates is a mature field with a decade of results. Every
one of those studies is a research project: a human frames the problem, defines the design
space, runs the solver, interprets the output. The solver sizes what it is given. **It does
not decide that this plate needs a rib at mid-span and that one needs its head split.**

> **Moosabeiki et al. 2023** — 3D-printed patient-specific plates, topology optimisation vs
> conventional design. [PMID 37866280](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37866280/)
>
> **Al-Tamimi 2021** — topology-optimised locking compression plates to reduce stress
> shielding. [PMID 34286146](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34286146/)

---

## B · What an autonomous loop changes

Three separate economies, worth keeping apart because they scale differently.
**None of the figures below are measured on this system yet** — section D says which numbers
are still missing.

### Time — calendar to clock

A human design review loop is bounded by working hours: propose, simulate, wait, meet, revise.
An agent loop is bounded by compute. It runs overnight, unattended, and the iteration budget
is a number in a config file rather than a scheduling problem.

The reduction is not "faster CAD". It is removing the human from the critical path *between*
iterations, so elapsed time stops being dominated by when people are awake.

### Money — roughly 200 sweep evaluations per agent turn

The design work splits in two:

| Decision type | Example | Who answers | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Shape** (topology) | rib or no rib, split the head, route further around the bone | the agent | one turn each |
| **Dimension** (scalar) | exact thickness, exact fillet radius | a numeric optimiser | a few hundred per turn |

Getting that split right is what makes the loop affordable: roughly five expensive decisions
instead of forty.

### Logistics — inventory to file

A hospital currently stocks many plate lengths and shapes per anatomy, plus the bending
instruments, and still sometimes lacks the right one. Patient-specific manufacture replaces a
physical catalogue with a design file and a printer.

The second logistical gain is documentary: **the commit history *is* the design history file**
— which check failed, what changed, what was rejected, what the numbers did after. That
artefact is mandatory for a real device and normally costs dedicated effort.

---

## C · What it changes for the operation itself

### A plate that already fits

The geometry is contoured to this patient's bone before it is manufactured, so the contouring
step leaves the operating room entirely. Fit stops depending on how much time is available and
who is doing the bending.

> **Zeng et al. 2016, *Injury*** — pre-bent plates shaped to the individual pelvis via 3D
> printing and virtual planning. [PMID 27372187](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27372187/)

### Fit that is deliberately imperfect

A plate pressed flat against bone crushes the periosteum and interrupts the blood supply the
fracture heals through — which is why limited-contact plates exist at all. The verifier bounds
the bone gap from **both** sides: at most 1.5 mm, and at least 0.1 mm. Zero clearance is
recorded as a failure, not an optimum.

> **Kregor et al. 1995, *J Orthop Res*** — LC-DCP designed to reduce cortical contact,
> ischaemia and porosis. [PMID 7472750](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7472750/)

### Strength is a window, not a maximum

The intuitive fix for a failing stress check — make it thicker — produces a clinically worse
device. An over-stiff plate carries load the bone should carry, the bone underneath resorbs,
and the construct fails later by a different route. That failure mode is documented in a
3D-printed titanium plate specifically, so the constraint set treats stiffness as a band with
both bounds binding.

> **Mie et al. 2020, *PLoS One*** — bone resorption, reduced BMD and degraded apatite
> orientation under a 3D-printed Ti-6Al-4V plate at 7 months, canine radius.
> [PMID 32877422](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32877422/)

### The surgical plan is an input, not an output

Screw positions and anatomical keep-out zones are supplied by the surgeon and locked. The
implant is required to accommodate them; the design loop cannot move a screw to make its own
life easier. Every planned trajectory is verified to pass cleanly through the finished solid.

> **Architectural, not measured.** Enforced by the locked-input allowlist. No clinical study
> attached — this is a property of the system, not a result.

---

## D · What we have not measured

An impact claim without this section is marketing. Everything above is either cited or
labelled architectural; here is the complete list of what remains unproven, including a flaw
in our own documentation.

- **No cost or wall-clock figure per validated design.** We have not yet measured compute cost
  per iteration, so the 200:1 ratio above is the designed intent of the two-tier split, not an
  observed result.
- **No operating-room time saved.** The mechanism is sound and the fit literature supports it,
  but we have measured nothing in a theatre and will not claim minutes.
- **Synthetic anatomy.** One procedurally generated femur. No patient data, no clinical
  validation, no FDA / ISO / ASTM claim of any kind.
- **Analytical stress model, not FEA.** Beam theory over cross-sections measured off the
  exported solid, with Heywood's net-section factor at the holes. Fast and honest about being
  a surrogate — but a confirming finite-element solve has not been run.
- **No fatigue analysis.** Bone plates fail by fatigue, not single overload. The safety factor
  of 2.5 exists to cover that, and a cyclic analysis is not a substitute for it — neither has
  been performed.
- **A claim in our own domain document is unsourced.** `DOMAIN_KNOWLEDGE.md` states that
  working length shifts axial stiffness by 28–37%. We could not find that figure, and the
  closest controlled study reports 10%. The direction is right; the magnitude is currently
  unsupported and flagged for correction.
  ([PMID 21185629](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21185629/))

---

## E · Taking it further

Ordered by what unblocks what. Phase 1 turns claims above into measurements; the later phases
widen the domain.

### Phase 1 — immediate: close the evidence gaps

- **One confirming FEA solve** on the final design — tetrahedral mesh, mesh-convergence table.
  The surrogate steers, the solver confirms.
- **A simulated standard bench test.** Four-point bending per the established metallic
  bone-plate method, reported as an engineer would receive it.
  ([PMID 24959354](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24959354/))
- **Instrument the loop.** Cost and elapsed time per validated design, so section B stops being
  an argument and becomes a number.

### Phase 2 — near term: from one case to a population

- **Real CT ingestion** end to end — segmentation, anatomical frame, quality gate — so the
  input is a scan rather than a generated mesh.
- **Batch across many patients** unattended, the only way to show generality rather than a
  single lucky convergence.
- **Fatigue as a first-class check**, since it is the real failure mode.
- **The verifier as a network service** the agent holds no credentials to, making the trust
  boundary physical rather than procedural.

### Phase 3 — beyond: other anatomies, species and domains

- **More anatomy** — the pipeline takes a mesh and a plan, so a different bone is a different
  input rather than a different program.
- **Vision in the loop.** Render the stress field onto the part and let the agent look at it.
  A coordinate is not actionable; a picture of where the plate narrows is.
- **Parallel design strategies.** When one approach stalls, try three structurally different
  ones at once and keep the best — recording the losers, which is itself evidence.

---

## F · Where else this goes

### Veterinary orthopaedics — *deployable first*

The strongest near-term application, and not as a consolation prize. Anatomical variation
across breeds and species destroys the economics of standard inventory — a plate range that
covers a dachshund and a great dane does not exist. The regulatory path is lighter, and the
system already routes non-human cases to autonomous release while human cases wait for a
signature. **Full autonomy is deployable here first.**

### Craniomaxillofacial reconstruction — *proven domain*

Already the home ground of patient-specific implants, already using topology optimisation, and
already accepting the cost of bespoke design. Exactly the domain where removing the
engineer-hours changes who can be treated rather than just how fast.

### Surgical guides and cutting jigs — *adjacent*

Osteotomy guides are geometry derived from a scan plus a plan, verified against clearances and
trajectories — structurally the same problem as the plate, with a lower consequence of failure
and a much shorter path to use.

### Any design problem with a frozen scorer — *the real result*

The transferable result is not the plate. It is the architecture: an agent that authors
geometry as code, a verifier it cannot edit, feedback carrying a measured value, a limit and a
location, and a mechanical allowlist proving it never touched the test. That pattern applies
wherever correctness is measurable and gaming the metric is the easy path — brackets, housings,
heat sinks, fixtures.

---

`4123303` is the best evidence you have that this is engineering rather than parameter search. The agent hit `bone_conformance_gap 4.646 mm` at a point where the plate was actually **0.4 mm off the bone** — and instead of tuning against a wrong number, it diagnosed *why the measurement was wrong*: neighbouring loft sections wobbling against each other at the scale of the segmentation ripple, producing a self-intersecting fold. `manifold_watertight` still passed because the tessellation closed. Then it fixed the seating surface, and — this is the part that matters — **rejected the obvious fix in writing**: a single global lift, priced by the worst point on the plate, would have spent 1.3 mm of gap at the distal end where the fit was already fine.

## It converged. On three cases, including a real CT.

```
21/21 on all three cases now, real-CT case included (was 18/21)
  analytic      53.956 g,  worst hole 299.2 MPa,  conformance 0.946/1.5
```

Every check green, under the 350 MPa allowable and the 55 g cap, on a femur segmented from a **public CT**.

## And the reason it converged is the interesting part

The agent found that `thickness_profile` was **overfitted to one patient**. It placed thickness at fixed fractions of plate length — fine for the screws it was tuned on. Import a different case and the inner holes land at s=0.22 and s=0.78, straddling the profile's 4.5 mm peak, so the plate reported 362–375 MPa on a 3.1 mm wall *while its thickest section carried no hole at all*.

The fix replaced pinned control points with two derived mechanisms:

- **`_moment_thickness`** — wall derived from *this plan's* screw span. Moment full at mid-footprint, zero at the outermost screws, thickness rising with it. Its own words: *"Nothing in the profile is patient-specific any more, so the rule survives a restart from the base case on a different scan."*
- **`_hole_bosses`** — cosine-tapered pads at each bore, with the mass arithmetic stated: reaching that wall by thickening the whole plate costs **~4 g**; six local pads cost **~0.6 g**.

That's the section-modulus argument from your own `DOMAIN_KNOWLEDGE.md` §5, applied correctly and priced. The agent generalised from a fitted constant to a rule, then justified locality by the mass budget. That's not parameter search.

import re, pathlib
p = pathlib.Path("autoimplants/viewer_template.html")
s = p.read_text(encoding="utf-8")

blocks = re.findall(r"<<<<<<< HEAD\n(.*?)=======\n(.*?)>>>>>>> origin/main\n", s, re.S)
print("conflicts found:", len(blocks))

resolved = []
for i, (ours, theirs) in enumerate(blocks):
    o = [l for l in ours.strip("\n").split("\n") if l.strip()]
    t = [l for l in theirs.strip("\n").split("\n") if l.strip()]
    if i == 0:
        # ours: animated reveal() (keep) | theirs: use-demo with demo/plan state (keep)
        merged = [o[0], t[1]]
    else:
        # ours: updateStageProgress + animated openWorkbench (keep both)
        # theirs: start-run with dicom/zip + surgical plan (keep)
        merged = [o[0], o[1], t[1]]
    resolved.append("\n".join(merged) + "\n")

out = s
for (ours, theirs), fix in zip(blocks, resolved):
    original = "<<<<<<< HEAD\n" + ours + "=======\n" + theirs + ">>>>>>> origin/main\n"
    out = out.replace(original, fix, 1)

assert "<<<<<<<" not in out and ">>>>>>>" not in out, "markers remain"
p.write_text(out, encoding="utf-8")
print("resolved, markers gone")
PY
